summary: Give the Electric potential calculator the relative permittivity, the charge 1, the charge 2 and the charge 3 and it returns distance (r). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Electric potential calculator work?
sections.html:
The Electric potential calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance (r) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of point charges); then you type in the relative permittivity (ϵᵣ), the charge 1 (q₁), the distance 1 (r₁) and the charge 2 (q₂).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Electric potential calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Distance (r)=charge (q) × constant ÷ electric potential (V)
Constant=8987551788 ÷ relative permittivity (ϵᵣ)
Electric potential (V)=(constant × (Electric pot system part 1 + Electric pot system part 2))
Charge 4 (q₄)=-charge 1 (q₁) × distance 4 (r₄) ÷ distance 1 (r₁) − charge 2 (q₂) × distance 4 (r₄) ÷ distance 2 (r₂) − charge 3 (q₃) × distance 4 (r₄) ÷ distance 3 (r₃) − charge 5 (q₅) × distance 4 (r₄) ÷ distance 5 (r₅) + distance 4 (r₄) × electric pot system part1
Electric pot system part 2=charge 10 (q₁₀) ÷ distance 10 (r₁₀) + charge 6 (q₆) ÷ distance 6 (r₆) + charge 7 (q₇) ÷ distance 7 (r₇) + charge 8 (q₈) ÷ distance 8 (r₈) + charge 9 (q₉) ÷ distance 9 (r₉)
Charge (q)=electric potential energy (U) ÷ electric potential difference (∆V)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Electric charge, opening in coulombs
  • Length, opening in micrometers

  • Electric charge, opening in coulombs

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Electric potential calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the relative permittivity, the charge 1 and the charge 2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Electric potential calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance (r), derived from the relative permittivity, the charge 1 and the charge 2. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Electric potential calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the relative permittivity, the charge 1, the charge 2 and the charge 3, which is 27 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter charge 1 (q₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Charge 1 (q₁) opens in coulombs and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Electric potential (V) = 0 × 10⁶. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Electric potential calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
